entry.title: What Is Tasti Tondi? Understanding the Legend That Inspired CZARD
entry.summary:
Explore the history of Tasti Tondi, the celebrated nickname of the Patek Philippe Ref. 1463, and discover how its enduring philosophy inspired CZARD's inaugural collection.

More
entry.content:
History rarely remembers every great watch.
It remembers the ones that quietly changed the direction of watchmaking.
The history of horology is often told through mechanical breakthroughs. New escapements improved precision. Automatic winding transformed convenience. Complications became increasingly sophisticated, demonstrating the ingenuity of Swiss engineering. Each generation introduced innovations that expanded what a wristwatch could accomplish.
Yet some of the most influential watches earned their place for a different reason.
They solved practical problems with uncommon intelligence. They demonstrated that engineering and design were not competing disciplines but complementary ones. Their influence extended far beyond their own production years, shaping how future generations thought about durability, proportion, and craftsmanship.
Few vintage chronographs illustrate this philosophy more convincingly than the Patek Philippe Reference 1463.
Introduced during the early 1940s, the Ref. 1463 represented far more than another manually wound chronograph from Geneva. It arrived at a moment when Swiss watchmaking was redefining the wristwatch-not only as a precision instrument but as an object expected to endure everyday life without sacrificing refinement. Its greatest achievement was addressing one of the era's most demanding engineering challenges: creating a chronograph that offered meaningful water resistance while preserving the elegance expected of Patek Philippe.
Over the decades, collectors came to know the watch by another name.
Tasti Tondi.
Today, the name has become inseparable from the reference itself, representing one of the defining chronographs in twentieth-century watchmaking.
Understanding its importance requires looking beyond rarity or auction records. The story begins in an era when chronographs were professional instruments rather than luxury objects and unfolds through advances in engineering, changing expectations of durability, and an enduring appreciation for thoughtful design.
The Ref. 1463 did not become historically important because it sought attention.
It became important because it quietly solved problems that many others had not.
That distinction transformed it from a successful chronograph into one of the most respected references in mechanical watchmaking.

Tasti Tondi ("round buttons") is the Italian nickname for the Patek Philippe Ref. 1463, a manually wound chronograph introduced in 1940. More than a beautiful vintage chronograph, it was one of the first serially produced water-resistant chronographs, remembered today not simply for its appearance, but for the engineering challenge it solved. 

Why the Nickname Stuck
Most great references are known by number. A small group earned names, and almost all of those names came from the same place: Italian collectors in the 1970s and 1980s, who turned catalogue numbers into things you could say out loud.
The Rolex comparison is helpful, but only up to a point. Paul Newman is not another word for the Daytona. It describes a specific exotic dial configuration found on a minority of Daytona references, which is precisely why it commands what it does. Tasti Tondi works differently. It names the whole reference, because on the Ref. 1463 the defining feature is structural rather than printed.
The naming convention stuck because the auction houses adopted it. Phillips catalogues the reference under the Tasti Tondi model name. Once the trade uses a collector nickname in official descriptions, it stops being slang and becomes part of the historical record.


More Than a Pair of Pushers
At first glance, naming one of history's most admired chronographs after the shape of its pushers might seem surprisingly modest.
Yet industrial design has often been shaped by precisely these kinds of details.
The rounded pushers of the Ref. 1463 were not memorable because they were decorative. They reflected a practical engineering solution. Chronograph pushers create openings in a watch case, and every opening presents another opportunity for dust or moisture to reach the movement.
Improving the construction of those pushers helped address one of the greatest technical challenges facing chronograph manufacturers during the period.
The rounded pushers became memorable because they represented a practical engineering solution. The nickname celebrates a visible detail, but the achievement it remembers is invisible: creating a chronograph that could better resist water and dust without compromising elegance. 
The beauty of the Ref. 1463 emerged not from ornament but from solving a technical problem with remarkable restraint.

A Different Era of Chronographs
Today, chronographs are admired as luxury watches, collector's pieces, and expressions of mechanical craftsmanship.
Before the Second World War, their purpose was considerably more practical.
Doctors measured pulse rates.
Pilots calculated navigation intervals.
Engineers timed industrial processes.
Scientists recorded experiments.
Military officers coordinated operations.
Sports officials measured athletic performance.
The chronograph existed because accurate elapsed time had practical value.
That purpose shaped every aspect of its design.
Early chronographs prioritised legibility over decoration. Cases remained relatively straightforward, while movements focused on reliability rather than visual complexity. Every additional component had to justify its existence.
The chronograph itself was already one of the most mechanically demanding complications of its era. Every press of a pusher initiated an intricate interaction between levers, springs, wheels, clutches, and hammers that had to operate with exceptional precision.
Making such a mechanism elegant was difficult.
Making it durable proved even harder.

The World Before the Ref. 1463
The decades leading to the introduction of the Ref. 1463 marked one of the most transformative periods in Swiss watchmaking.
The First World War accelerated the transition from pocket watches to wristwatches, encouraging manufacturers to rethink case construction, movement architecture, and ergonomics. Watches now accompanied their owners through daily life, exposed to dust and moisture. 
Chronographs evolved alongside these broader changes, but they faced engineering challenges that ordinary wristwatches did not.
A conventional watch required only a winding crown to pass through the case.
A chronograph required three moving controls-the crown and two pushers.
Every additional opening represented another potential path for moisture or contamination to reach the movement.
Achieving meaningful water resistance therefore required far more than a stronger case.
It demanded a complete rethinking of how the movement, crown, pushers, and case interacted as a single system.

The problem the 1463 was built to solve
A time-only wristwatch has one opening in its case: the winding stem. A chronograph has three, because each pusher needs its own tube through the case band. Every opening is a path for water and dust to reach a movement that will not tolerate either.
By the late 1930s this had become a commercial problem rather than a theoretical one. Sport and outdoor pursuits were fashionable, and buyers wanted a chronograph that could survive being worn rather than carried. Patek Philippe's existing chronographs, the Reference 130 of 1934 and the Reference 530 of 1937, were superb and comparatively fragile. The 1463 was conceived as the robust alternative to the 130, not as a technical showpiece.
The distinction matters. The 1463 was not built to demonstrate that Patek could do something difficult. It was built to solve a practical problem that customers increasingly faced: keeping water and dust out of a chronograph designed to be worn every day. 


The Specialists Behind the Ref. 1463
By the early 1940s, Swiss watchmaking had evolved into a highly specialised industry. Few manufacturers produced every component themselves. Movements, dials, hands, cases, and crystals were often entrusted to independent firms whose expertise had been refined over generations.
For Patek Philippe, this approach was not a compromise but a strength. Rather than attempting to master every discipline in-house, the manufacture collaborated with specialists capable of producing components to its exacting standards.
The Ref. 1463 demonstrates this philosophy particularly well. Its movement came from within Patek Philippe's established chronograph programme. Still, the case-the component responsible for protecting that movement from dust and moisture-was entrusted to Frères Borges, later Taubert & Fils, one of Geneva's foremost specialists in water-resistant case construction. 
That decision reveals something important about the watch itself. The Ref. 1463 did not become historically significant because every component was made under one roof. Its significance lies in how specialist expertise came together to solve a complex engineering problem, producing a chronograph whose whole was greater than the sum of its individual parts. 

The Birth of the Ref. 1463
By the early 1940s, Swiss watchmaking had reached an important turning point. Precision alone was no longer enough to distinguish the finest manufactures. Collectors and professionals increasingly expected watches that combined mechanical sophistication with durability, everyday practicality, and refined design.
It was within this environment that Patek Philippe introduced the Reference 1463.
Widely regarded as the manufacture's first serially produced water-resistant chronograph wristwatch, the Ref. 1463 demonstrated that technical innovation did not have to come at the expense of refinement. Rather than reinventing the chronograph, it solved one of the era's most demanding engineering problems while preserving the restrained proportions and elegance for which Patek Philippe was already respected.
That balance between engineering and design became the defining characteristic of the Ref. 1463, securing its place among the most important chronographs of the twentieth century. 


The Case, and the Firm That Actually Made It 
Patek Philippe did not manufacture the case itself, and that is often the part left out of the story. 
The 1463 case was supplied by Frères Borges, later Taubert, a Geneva casemaker that specialised in etanche, or sealed, construction. Their FB stamp sits inside the case back. The reference owes much of its historical significance to Patek Philippe's decision to work with an outside specialist for the component that defined its water-resistant construction. 
The construction was three-piece, with a screw-down case back and a soft iron inner dust cover that also gave the movement a degree of antimagnetic protection. The pushers were made large, round and fluted for two reasons at once: the increased circumference gave a longer sealing surface against the pusher tube, and the fluting gave a wet or gloved finger something to grip. Neither decision was aesthetic. Both became the watch's signature.
Case production divides into two broad series, distinguished by lug profile and traceable through serial ranges, with the earlier examples showing a gentler lug curve. Collector research also identifies a small number of FB cases with a flat bezel rather than the more familiar stepped profile, although these examples remain comparatively uncommon. 
The significance of the Ref. 1463 therefore lies not in the movement alone, but in the successful integration of movement, case, and engineering into a watch that could withstand everyday wear without compromising refinement. 

A New Standard for Chronographs
Rather than treating water resistance as an additional feature, Patek Philippe approached the Ref. 1463 as an integrated system. The case, pushers, crown, and movement were designed to work together, improving everyday durability while preserving the restrained proportions expected of one of Geneva's foremost manufactures.
Its engineering quietly shaped its appearance rather than dominating it. . Yet beneath its restrained exterior, the Ref. 1463 represented a new standard for what a serially produced chronograph could be: elegant enough for formal wear, yet robust enough for everyday use.
Its influence extended well beyond its own production years. Later water-resistant chronographs would follow different technical paths, but the Ref. 1463 had already demonstrated that engineering innovation and refined design were not competing ideals. They could exist within the same watch, each strengthening the other.

Patek Philippe's Mid-Century Chronograph Evolution
Viewed together, four references illustrate the evolution of Patek Philippe's chronograph philosophy.
Reference
Historical Importance
Ref. 130
Established Patek Philippe's early chronograph language and laid the foundation for future chronograph development.
Ref. 1463
Widely recognised as Patek Philippe's first serially produced water-resistant chronograph, combining technical innovation with elegant case design.
Ref. 1563
An exceptionally rare split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph that expanded upon the engineering principles introduced by the Ref. 1463.
Ref. 5070
A modern manually wound chronograph that reflects the balanced proportions and restrained design language of Patek Philippe's celebrated mid-century references.

Rather than representing isolated milestones, these references chart the gradual refinement of Patek Philippe's approach to the chronograph across several decades.

Design Language: Why the Ref. 1463 Endures
Many vintage watches belong unmistakably to their era. The Ref. 1463 continues to feel contemporary because its proportions were guided by function rather than fashion.
Its appeal lies in the way every component works together. The case, bezel, dial, lugs, and rounded pushers form a balanced composition in which no element dominates another.
That quiet restraint explains why the Ref. 1463 remains one of the defining chronographs of twentieth-century watchmaking.

The Rounded Pushers
The rounded pushers became the defining visual characteristic of the Ref. 1463 and the origin of its "Tasti Tondi" nickname. Their larger, fluted construction improved grip while providing more substantial sealing surfaces, helping address one of the principal engineering challenges of waterproof chronographs. Over time, this practical solution became the watch's most recognisable visual signature.
Case Proportions
Modern watches often pursue wrist presence through diameter.
The Ref. 1463 achieves presence through proportion.
The relationship between bezel width, dial opening, lug length, and case thickness creates a watch that appears balanced from every angle without feeling oversized or compressed.

The Bezel
The polished bezel performs a remarkably restrained role.
Rather than dominating the watch, it frames the dial with quiet precision, naturally directing attention toward the chronograph display.
Its simplicity is one of its greatest strengths.

Dial Architecture
Designing a successful chronograph dial requires organising a considerable amount of information without overwhelming the wearer.
Elapsed time.
Running seconds.
Scale markings.
Hour markers.
Brand signature.
The Ref. 1463 resolves this challenge through careful organisation rather than reduction. Its chronograph registers create immediate visual balance, while generous spacing keeps the dial clear and legible.

Typography, Lugs & Crystal
Restrained typography reinforces readability while establishing a natural rhythm across the dial. The lugs extend organically from the case, creating a seamless transition to the strap while improving comfort and balance. Above the dial, the gently domed crystal introduces subtle depth without compromising legibility.
Together, these restrained details create one of the most harmonious chronograph designs of the twentieth century.

Engineering Behind the Watch
The elegance visible on the outside concealed an extraordinary amount of mechanical thought beneath the dial.
A manually wound chronograph remains one of traditional watchmaking's most sophisticated mechanisms.
Every press of the upper pusher activates a coordinated sequence of levers, wheels, springs, clutches, and hammers.
The chronograph seconds hand begins its sweep.
Another press stops the mechanism.
A final press returns every indication precisely to zero.
Even the slightest deviation in adjustment could affect reliability or accuracy, demanding exceptional craftsmanship during the 1940s.


Building a Water-Resistant Chronograph
The defining technical accomplishment of the Ref. 1463 lay not inside its movement but around it.
Every opening into the case represented a potential weakness requiring tighter machining tolerances and more sophisticated sealing.
Case makers refined component fit.
Engineers improved sealing surfaces.
Manufacturing precision advanced steadily.
Together, these improvements demonstrated that meaningful water resistance could coexist with elegant case design, influencing chronograph development for decades.

Variations & the Rare Reference 1563
The Ref. 1463 remained in production for more than two decades, evolving gradually rather than through dramatic redesign.
Examples appeared in yellow gold, pink gold, and stainless steel, while subtle changes in dial layouts, scale configurations, and retailer signatures reflected the realities of traditional Swiss production.
Closely related was the exceptionally rare Reference 1563, a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph that expanded upon the same waterproof case philosophy while preserving the disciplined design language established by the Ref. 1463.


Collectors, Legacy & CZARD's Interpretation
Vintage collecting has never been solely about rarity.
The Ref. 1463 continues to be admired because it brings together historical importance, mechanical sophistication, disciplined design, and long-term usability in a remarkably coherent whole.
That balance explains why discussions surrounding the reference begin with its historical contribution before turning to its market value.

Why Collectors Still Admire the Tasti Tondi
Vintage collecting has never been solely about rarity.
Many watches survive in very small numbers.
Only a select few continue to attract equal admiration from historians, designers, restorers, and collectors.
The Ref. 1463 belongs firmly within that group.
Its significance comes from the unusual combination of qualities it represents.
Historical importance.
Mechanical sophistication.
Exceptional case construction.
Disciplined design.
Long-term usability.
Rather than excelling in one area alone, the Ref. 1463 brought these qualities together in a remarkably coherent whole. That balance explains why discussions surrounding the reference almost always begin with its historical contribution before turning to its market value.

Originality Over Perfection
One of the most significant changes in vintage collecting has been the growing appreciation for originality.
Earlier generations often restored watches until they appeared almost new.
Modern scholarship takes a different approach.
Collectors increasingly value watches that retain their original dial, hands, case geometry, and finishing, even when decades of careful wear remain visible.
The Ref. 1463 illustrates this philosophy particularly well.
These signs of age are not imperfections.
They are historical evidence.

Scholarship Beyond the Auction Room
Auction catalogues today serve a purpose far beyond facilitating sales.
Institutions such as Phillips, Christie's, and Sotheby's increasingly publish detailed historical research alongside exceptional examples of important watches. Production periods are compared, dial variations documented, retailer signatures examined, and provenance carefully recorded.
Each newly documented Ref. 1463 contributes another piece to the historical record.


Beyond Horology: Lessons in Design
The influence of the Ref. 1463 extends beyond watchmaking.
Industrial designers study it as an example of disciplined product development, where every visible element serves a clear purpose.
That philosophy explains why the Ref. 1463 still feels contemporary despite originating during the early 1940s.

An Enduring Influence
The Ref. 1463 also influenced the manufacture's own chronograph development.
Later Patek Philippe references introduced new complications, larger cases, and evolving aesthetics, yet many retained the disciplined approach to proportion established during the mid-century.
Modern references such as the Reference 5070 acknowledge this design philosophy while interpreting it for a different generation of collectors
These ideas remain as relevant today as they were when the Ref. 1463 first appeared.

CZARD's Interpretation
Historic watches deserve respect because they belong to a specific moment in the evolution of watchmaking.
They reflect the manufacturing techniques, engineering priorities, and aesthetic values of their own time.
Attempting to recreate them exactly risks reducing history to nostalgia.
CZARD approaches that history differently.
The Ref. 1463 is studied not as a blueprint to copy but as an example of thoughtful watchmaking. Its balanced proportions, disciplined case architecture, and engineering-first philosophy provide principles to interpret rather than forms to reproduce.
For CZARD, the objective is not to recreate a historical reference but to understand the thinking behind it and apply those enduring principles to contemporary watchmaking.
History deserves interpretation, not imitation.

Respecting Heritage Without Recreating It
Every generation inherits more than manufacturing techniques.
It inherits ideas.
Ideas about craftsmanship.
Ideas about mechanical integrity.
Ideas about proportion.
Ideas about restraint.
The most enduring watchmakers have rarely advanced the craft by ignoring history.
Instead, they studied it carefully before contributing something of their own.
That same philosophy guides CZARD.
Rather than pursuing nostalgia, the brand studies the principles that allowed references such as the Ref. 1463 to endure. It seeks to understand why those principles remain relevant before interpreting them through a modern perspective.
History is not something to repeat.
It is something to learn from.

Conclusion
Some watches become valuable.
Far fewer become historically important.
The distinction matters because markets change.
History rarely does.
The Patek Philippe Reference 1463 earned its place in horology not through extravagance or mechanical excess, but by solving one of its era's most demanding engineering challenges with remarkable discipline. It demonstrated that a chronograph could become more practical without sacrificing refinement, establishing principles that continue to influence collectors, designers, and watchmakers more than eighty years later.
The nickname Tasti Tondi refers only to its rounded pushers.
Its legacy is far broader.
It represents a moment when engineering shaped design rather than competing with it-when craftsmanship served function, and every visible detail existed because it had a purpose.
For CZARD, the Ref. 1463 is neither a destination nor a template.
It is a reminder that enduring design begins with careful observation, thoughtful engineering, and respect for the work that came before.
The Tasti Tondi remains influential not because later watches resemble it, but because it demonstrated that disciplined engineering and purposeful design need never compete.
More than eighty years later, that lesson continues to guide collectors, historians, and modern watchmakers alike.

entry.title: Not a Customer. A Collector. The Philosophy Behind CZARD
entry.summary:
At CZARD, owning a watch begins with a purchase, but becoming a collector begins with a shared appreciation for craftsmanship, history, and the journey of the House.

 

More
entry.content:
A Word Worth Refusing

Most brands have customers. CZARD does not.

This is not a matter of vanity, and it is not a marketing flourish. It is a decision about the kind of relationship a House wants to have with the people who wear its watches. The word you choose for someone quietly decides how you treat them, and how they come to see themselves. So we chose a different word, and we hold to it everywhere. At CZARD, there are no customers. There are Collectors.

The distinction sounds small. Its consequences are not.

What a Customer Is

A customer is defined by a transaction. The word describes a moment: money changes hands, a product is delivered, and the relationship, in the strict sense of the word, is complete. A customer is someone a business has, and once the sale is made, the language has nothing more to say.

There is nothing wrong with the word in most of commerce. It is honest about what most commerce is. But it carries an assumption underneath it, that the object is the end of the story, and the person is the means to a sale. For a House built on the idea that a watch is the beginning of something, not the end, that assumption is exactly backwards.

What a Collector Is

A collector is not defined by a purchase. A collector is defined by a relationship to what they own, one that begins at acquisition and deepens over time.

Collectors do not simply hold objects. They hold context: why a piece matters, where it sits in a larger story, what it will mean in twenty years. They think in terms of provenance, permanence, and place. The object is not the end of the relationship. It is the reason the relationship exists.

That is the word CZARD chose, because it is the truer description of what we hope owning a CZARD becomes. Not a purchase that concludes, but a place taken in a story that continues.

Why the Word Changes Everything

Language is not decoration. The word a House uses for its people shapes every decision it makes about them.

A brand that thinks in customers optimises for the sale: the conversion, the checkout, the next transaction. A House that thinks in Collectors optimises for the decade: the record that outlives the receipt, the value that holds, the reason to remain proud of a piece long after the moment of buying it has passed. The same watch, sold to a customer or entrusted to a Collector, is treated as two different things by the House behind it.

So the change from customer to Collector is not cosmetic. It is a commitment. It obliges us to build for permanence rather than for the sale, and to honour the people who chose us early for as long as the House exists.

The Collector and the Chapter

Every Collector enters the House at a particular moment, and that moment gives them their place. It decides their chapter, and their number within it, a position no one else will ever hold. The mechanics of how that works, the sealed chapters, the single running sequence, the number that exists only once, are described in The CZARD Chapter System. What matters here is simpler: a Collector is not an anonymous buyer of a product. A Collector is a named place in a story with a beginning, a middle, and no end.

You cannot choose your chapter. Your time chooses it for you. That is true of every Collector, and it is why the relationship is never a transaction. You are not buying a position in the market. You are taking a position in a history.

Member of a House

There is one more word CZARD uses, and it belongs beside Collector: Member. To own a CZARD is to become a Chapter Member, part of the group of people who share a chapter and, through it, a moment in the life of the House.

That is the quiet promise underneath the terminology. A customer is someone a company has. A Collector, a Member, is someone a House keeps. The first relationship ends at the sale. The second is only beginning there.

This is why the word matters enough to refuse the alternative. Call someone a customer and you have described a transaction. Call them a Collector and you have described a belonging. CZARD was built for the second.

Enter the House of CZARD

 

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does CZARD call buyers Collectors instead of customers?

Because the relationship is not a transaction. A customer is defined by a purchase that concludes; a Collector is defined by an ongoing relationship to what they own. The word reflects how CZARD treats the people who wear its watches, as members of a House, not the end of a sale.

What is a Chapter Member?

Every CZARD owner belongs to a chapter of the House, and shares that chapter with the other Collectors in it. That shared place makes each owner a Chapter Member, part of a specific moment in CZARD’s history.

Is this just a marketing term?

No. The choice of word shapes how the House operates: building for permanence and long-term ownership rather than optimising for the sale. It is a commitment to the Collector, not a label.

How does someone become a CZARD Collector?

By acquiring a CZARD timepiece, which gives the owner a numbered place within a chapter of the House. That number, and the chapter it belongs to, are theirs alone.

entry.title: Built to Be Passed On: The Legacy of Every CZARD Watch
entry.summary:
Discover why every CZARD watch is designed to outlive its first owner, becoming a legacy that can be preserved, inherited, and remembered across generations.

More
entry.content:
The Watches We Keep

Most objects are bought to be used and, eventually, replaced. A few are bought to be kept. Fewer still are made to be handed to someone else one day.

A watch is one of the rare things a person can own for a lifetime and then give away without it being any less theirs for having been given. It does not wear out with a season. It does not become obsolete when the next model arrives. Worn carefully and serviced when it needs it, a well-made watch can outlast the person who first chose it, and that is precisely what makes it worth choosing.

Every CZARD is built with that second life in mind. Not a watch to be replaced, but a watch to be passed on.

An Object Becomes an Heirloom

An heirloom is not a category of object. It is an ordinary object that time and meaning have turned into something more.

A watch becomes an heirloom the same way anything does. It is present for the moments that matter, it is kept rather than discarded, and one day it is handed to someone who will carry it forward. The watch itself does not change. What changes is everything that gathers around it: the wrist it was on, the years it measured, the person who wore it before.

This is why a watch built for permanence matters more than one built for a moment. A piece designed to be replaced can never become an heirloom, because it is not meant to survive long enough to become one. A piece designed to last is given the chance. Whether it takes that chance is up to the people who own it, but the design has to allow for it first.

A Number That Stays With the Watch

Every CZARD carries a number that belongs to the watch itself, not to whoever happens to own it at a given moment. The chapter and number, described in The CZARD Chapter System, are fixed for the life of the piece. They do not reset when the watch changes hands.

That permanence is what makes a CZARD suited to being passed on. When a watch moves from one person to the next, whether from a parent to a child or between two collectors, its identity travels with it, unchanged. The number that marked its place in the history of the House on the day it was made marks that same place decades later, in different hands. The owner may change. The watch’s place in the story never does.

Ownership That Can Move Forward

A watch that is meant to be inherited needs more than durable parts. It needs a way for its ownership to move forward honestly, so that the person who receives it holds not just the watch, but its history.

CZARD is building a record for exactly this purpose. One day, the House will be able to recognise every transfer of ownership, allowing the history of a watch to continue alongside the watch itself, so that a father can hand a CZARD to a son and have that moment become part of the piece’s story rather than lost to it. That system is still being built. The principle behind it already exists: a CZARD is designed to be owned more than once, and to be worthy of each owner in turn.

Why Legacy Cannot Be Rushed

No brand can manufacture an heirloom. It can only build something worthy of becoming one, and then let time do the rest.

That is the honest limit of what any House can promise. We cannot make your CZARD meaningful to the person you give it to; only your life with it can do that. What we can do is build a watch that will still be running, still be legible, and still hold its place in a story when that day comes, so that when you pass it on, there is something real to pass on. Permanence is the House’s responsibility. Meaning is yours to add.

A watch built to be replaced asks only to be bought. A watch built to be passed on asks to be lived with, and then given. CZARD was made for the second kind of ownership, the kind that does not end with you.

One day, someone else may wear your CZARD. They will inherit more than a watch. They will inherit the years you entrusted to it. That is what makes an heirloom.

Enter the House of CZARD

Frequently Asked Questions

Are CZARD watches designed to be passed down?

Yes. CZARD watches are built for permanence rather than replacement, with the intention that they can be worn for a lifetime and then handed to the next owner or the next generation.

Does a CZARD keep its number when it changes hands?

Yes. The chapter and number belong to the watch itself, not to the current owner. They stay fixed for the life of the piece, so a watch’s identity and place in the House travel with it when it is passed on.

Can ownership of a CZARD be transferred or recorded?

A permanent record is being built to recognise when a watch passes from one owner to the next, so its lineage can be part of its story. This record is forthcoming and not yet live; the principle it serves, that a CZARD is made to be owned more than once, is already part of the design.

What makes a watch a good heirloom?

Durability, timeless legibility, and a fixed identity that survives changing hands. A piece built for permanence can become an heirloom over time; a piece built to be replaced cannot.

entry.title: The Coin and the Certificate: The Symbols of Ownership at CZARD
entry.summary:
Discover why every CZARD watch is accompanied by a numbered coin and certificate, physical symbols of ownership that preserve your place in the history of the House.

 

 

More
entry.content:
A Number Needs More Than a Watch

A number is a quiet thing. Engraved on a caseback, it can be seen only by the person who takes the watch off and turns it over. It is real, but it is hidden, and a place in history deserves to be held in the hand as well as worn on the wrist.

That is why every CZARD arrives with more than the watch. It comes with two companions, a coin and a certificate, that give the number a physical form. The number itself, and how it is assigned, is explained in The CZARD Chapter System. This is about the two objects that make it something you can hold.

The Coin: A Number You Can Hold

The coin is the number made tangible. Where the engraving on the caseback is private, the coin is a thing you can keep, show, and pass across a table: a small, deliberate object that says, in effect, this number is mine.

It is meant to carry the identity plainly. To hold the coin is to hold proof that you are, for example, A-127, the one hundred and twenty-seventh watch of Chapter A, a position no one else in the history of the House will ever occupy. A watch tells the time to everyone who sees it. The coin tells your place in the story to you.

That is the quiet power of a separate object. The watch is worn and admired for what it is. The coin exists for what it means. Together they say two different things: one measures your days, the other marks your place.

The Certificate: A Place in the House, Written Down

If the coin is the emblem of ownership, the certificate is its record. It sets down, in writing, exactly what you hold: the maison, the collection, the model, the chapter, and the number, the full identity of your watch expressed as a single, unrepeatable line.

A certificate like this does more than confirm a purchase. It states a right. It says that within CZARD, this specific number belongs to you, completely and permanently, and that no other watch in the House carries it or ever will. It is the difference between owning a product and holding a documented place in history.

And a certificate is built to outlast the moment it was issued. Long after the day of acquisition is forgotten, the certificate remains, ready to speak for the watch and its owner. That is why it is treated not as paperwork, but as part of the piece itself.

Why the Signature Matters

The most personal mark on a certificate is the one made by a human hand.

A printed name is a formality. A genuine signature is a gesture, one person putting their name to an object and vouching for it. When a certificate carries a real, handwritten signature from the House, it becomes a small act of trust between the maker and the owner, not a mass-produced document but a personal acknowledgement that this watch, this number, belongs to this person. It is a slower, more deliberate way of doing things, and that is exactly the point.

Physical Today, Verifiable Tomorrow

The coin and the certificate are physical, and they are given with the watch. They are real, present objects, held in the hand from the first day of ownership.

In time, they will be joined by a digital companion. A permanent record is being built so that the same identity, chapter, number, certificate, and the watch’s history can be verified online for decades, long after the day of purchase. The physical and the digital are meant to reinforce one another: the coin and certificate you can hold, and a record you can point to, so that in ten or twenty years the authenticity of a watch can be confirmed by anyone, anywhere. That digital record is still being built. The physical proof already exists, in your hand.

What Ownership Should Feel Like

There is a difference between buying something and being given a place in something. The coin and the certificate exist to mark that difference.

They turn a private number into something you can hold, show, and one day pass on. They state, in metal and on paper, that a specific position in the history of CZARD is yours alone. And they make ownership feel like what it is meant to be at a House: not the end of a transaction, but the beginning of a belonging.

The watch keeps your time. The coin and the certificate keep your place.

Enter the House of CZARD

 

Frequently Asked Questions

What comes with a CZARD watch?

Every CZARD arrives with the watch, a numbered coin, and a certificate. Together they give you a place within the CZARD Chapter System, with a number tied to your watch

What is the CZARD coin?

A small, keepable object that carries your watch’s identity, for example A-127. It makes your place in the House tangible, separate from the number engraved on the caseback.

What does the certificate confirm?

It records the full identity of your watch, the maison, collection, model, chapter, and number, and states that this specific number belongs to you and to no other watch in the House.

entry.title: VICI: The Story Behind the Word, and Why History Remembered It
entry.summary:
Discover the meaning behind VICI, the final word in Caesar's famous phrase, and explore how its philosophy of lasting achievement continues to inspire the vision of CZARD.

More
entry.content:
The Only Word Caesar Did Not Control

Three words complete the phrase. Only one became a verdict.

Caesar could choose to arrive. He could choose to assess. Both were within his power, both were the result of preparation, and both would have been true whatever happened next.

The third word is different. Vici does not describe an action. It describes an outcome, and an outcome is never entirely the property of the person who produced it. Caesar could decide to march and decide to look. He could not decide to have conquered.

That distinction is easy to miss, because victory is the word everyone remembers and the one that gets repeated. It sits at the end of the sentence in the position of triumph.

It is also the word that depended most on everything preceding it, and the only one whose meaning was settled by other people.

What Did Vici Actually Mean?

Vici is the first-person singular perfect of the Latin verb vincere, to conquer or to overcome.

The verb has travelled further into modern language than either of the others. It gives us victory and victor, invincible and evict. It also gives us convince, from com and vincere, meaning to overcome thoroughly. To convince someone, in the original sense, was to defeat their position rather than persuade them out of it.

That range is worth noticing. Vincere was never confined to warfare. It described the act of prevailing over resistance of any kind, which is why the word survives in contexts that have nothing to do with armies.

Latin treated conquest and persuasion as versions of the same thing.

The Victory That Should Have Been Forgotten

Here is the part of the story that is rarely told.

Zela was not an important battle.

Caesar's conquest of Gaul ran for the better part of a decade and reshaped Western Europe. His crossing of the Rubicon changed the constitutional future of Rome. His campaign in Egypt altered the politics of the eastern Mediterranean. Against these, a short engagement against Pharnaces II in 47 BC was a minor episode in a long career.

By any military measure, Zela should have disappeared into the record along with dozens of other campaigns whose names survive only in specialist scholarship.

It did not disappear, and the reason has nothing to do with the fighting.

It survived because of the sentence.

Why the Sentence Outlived the Conquest

Three verbs. No description of the terrain, no account of strategy, no praise of the commander, no casualty figures. Nothing that a military report of the period would normally contain.

Ancient sources differ on how the phrase first appeared. Plutarch describes it in a brief written report sent to Rome. Appian connects it to Caesar's written account. Suetonius records it displayed as an inscription during the Pontic Triumph. The details vary and the character does not.

What made it last was compression. Caesar reported a campaign in three words and left everything else out, and the omissions are what gave the phrase its force. A longer account would have been accurate and forgotten.

There is a lesson in that which has very little to do with Rome. The work is one thing. What survives of it is another, and the two are decided by different people at different times.

Caesar won at Zela. Everyone else decided that the sentence was worth keeping.

What Victory Actually Is

Not the moment it happens.

A victory is a verdict, and verdicts are delivered by people other than the person being judged, usually later, and frequently for reasons the person would not have chosen. Caesar was assassinated three years after Zela. Whatever he had conquered did not protect him, and the Republic he had fought over did not survive the men who killed him to preserve it.

That is the ordinary shape of it. You do the work, and then it passes out of your hands.

This is why the final word in the phrase is the least reliable of the three. Arrival can be planned. Assessment can be practised. Victory can only be attempted, and its meaning is assigned afterwards by people with their own reasons.

Anyone who has made something and released it knows the feeling. The object leaves the workshop finished, and what it becomes is no longer a decision you get to make.

Why CZARD Chose VICI

The trilogy runs in sequence because the sequence is the argument.

VENI is the decision to begin, taken before the outcome is known. VIDI is the long stretch of judgement that produces nothing visible. VICI is the point at which the work stops being yours.

For a watchmaker, that is the moment a watch leaves. Every proportion has been settled, every element that did not earn its place has been removed, and there is nothing further to be decided. What happens next belongs to whoever wears it.

VICI carries an oxford green dial, the deepest of the three, where the light has to be found rather than given. It is the least immediate of the collection, rewarding attention over first impressions.

The pairing felt less like a decision than a consequence.

A watch is not finished when the maker lets it go.

It is finished when someone chooses to keep wearing it.

Arrival belongs to the maker.

Understanding belongs to the craft.

Recognition belongs to everyone else.

That is VICI.

Discover VICI

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Vici mean?
Vici is Latin for "I conquered," the first-person singular perfect of the verb vincere, meaning to conquer or overcome. The same root gives English victory, invincible and convince.

What does Veni, Vidi, Vici mean?
"I came, I saw, I conquered." The phrase is attributed to Julius Caesar and describes his rapid defeat of Pharnaces II at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC.

Was the Battle of Zela an important victory?
 Not by military standards. It was a comparatively minor campaign set against Caesar's conquest of Gaul or his crossing of the Rubicon. It is remembered because of the sentence that followed it rather than the battle itself.

Where does the word convince come from?
From the Latin com and vincere, meaning to overcome thoroughly. In its original sense, to convince someone was to defeat their position rather than persuade them from it.

Why did CZARD name a watch VICI?
 VICI marks the point at which work passes out of the maker's hands and its value is decided by others. It is the final chapter in a trilogy following the sequence of the phrase itself, after VENI, the decision to begin, and VIDI, the judgement that precedes any result.

entry.title: VIDI: The Story Behind the Word, and Why It Mattered More Than Victory
entry.summary:
Discover the deeper meaning of VIDI, the second word in Julius Caesar's famous phrase, and explore how observation, clarity, and conviction inspired one of CZARD's chronograph collections.

More
entry.content:
The Middle Word

Three words, and almost everyone remembers two of them.

Veni is the beginning, and beginnings are easy to admire. Vici is the ending, and endings are what history records. Between them sits a word that receives almost no attention at all, despite being the one that made the other two possible.

Vidi. I saw.

It is the least dramatic verb in the sentence. Nothing happens when you see something. No ground is covered, no outcome is decided, no victory is won. Seeing produces nothing that anyone can point to afterwards.

Yet remove it and the phrase collapses. Arrival alone changes nothing. Victory without understanding is luck.

The middle word is where the work happens, and it is almost always the part left out of the story.

What Did Vidi Actually Mean?

Vidi is the first-person singular perfect of the Latin verb videre, and the direct translation is simply "I saw."

The verb carried more weight than the English translation suggests. Videre meant to see, but it also meant to perceive, to consider, to understand. The same root gives us evidence, vision, provide, prudent. To have seen something, in Latin, implied more than the physical act of looking at it.

The connection runs deeper than Latin. The same ancient linguistic root also gave rise to the Sanskrit Veda, meaning knowledge, and English words such as wise and wit. Across cultures, seeing and knowing were rarely treated as separate ideas.

That is what Caesar's middle word is doing. He is not reporting that he looked at a battlefield. He is reporting that he understood it.

Why Seeing Was the Difficult Part

In the autumn of 47 BC, Caesar reached Zela to confront Pharnaces II. The battle itself was brief enough that the campaign became a byword for speed.

The speed was possible because of what happened before it. Caesar's method depended on knowing the ground before committing to it. Scouts mapped terrain in advance, rivers and elevation were studied as active participants in a campaign rather than as scenery, and every unknown that could be resolved beforehand was one fewer remaining once the fighting began. At Zela that work showed. He took the higher ground and attacked before his opponent could use his own position.

None of this appears in the phrase. Vidi compresses weeks of assessment into a single syllable, which is exactly how the work of understanding is usually recorded: briefly, if at all.

Why the Middle Step Disappears From Every Story

Because it produces nothing visible.

An architect studies a site for months and the drawings show none of it. A writer rereads a manuscript twenty times and the reader sees only the version that survived. A watchmaker examines a dial through a loupe, sets it aside, and examines the next one, and the finished watch carries no record of the ones rejected.

Assessment leaves no evidence behind. What it leaves is the absence of mistakes, and absence is not something anyone can admire.

This is why cultures reward decisiveness and rarely reward judgement. Decisiveness can be seen. Judgement can only be inferred, usually much later, from the fact that something worked.

The habit of looking properly before acting is among the least glamorous of all disciplines, and among the few that reliably separate work that lasts from work that does not.

What Vidi Asks of Anyone

Not patience, exactly. Patience implies waiting, and waiting is passive.

Vidi asks for something more demanding: the willingness to spend time understanding a problem while producing nothing, and the confidence that the time is not being wasted.

That is uncomfortable. There is a strong pull toward visible activity, because visible activity looks like progress and can be reported. Study looks like delay. In most rooms, the person who moves first is credited with initiative, and the person who understood the situation best is credited with nothing.

Caesar's phrase quietly disagrees. He put seeing in the middle, between arriving and winning, because that is where it belongs. Not as a preliminary to the real work, but as the step on which the outcome depended.

Anyone who has made something well recognises the pattern. The decision that mattered was made long before anyone was watching.

Why CZARD Chose VIDI

The trilogy is named in sequence because the sequence is the argument.

VENI is the decision to begin, made before the outcome is known. VICI is the result, judged by others long afterwards. VIDI is what happens in between, and it is the part of making anything that consumes the most time and receives the least credit.

On VIDI, clarity became the governing principle. The ivory dial leaves nowhere for imbalance to hide. Every proportion, every register and every line is exposed, making restraint more important than decoration. Most of that work was not about adding detail, but removing anything that did not deserve to remain.

The watch does not announce the work behind it. Nothing well made ever does.

Every achievement begins with arrival. Every achievement ends with recognition.

Between them lies the work almost nobody sees.

That is VIDI.

Discover VIDI

Frequently Asked Questions

What does Vidi mean?
Vidi is Latin for "I saw," the first-person singular perfect of the verb videre. The verb also carried meanings of perceiving and understanding, so the word implies comprehension rather than only sight.

What does Veni, Vidi, Vici mean?
"I came, I saw, I conquered." The phrase is attributed to Julius Caesar and summarises his swift victory over Pharnaces II at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC.

Why is Vidi the most overlooked word in the phrase?
 Because it describes assessment rather than action. Arrival and victory are both visible events, while understanding produces nothing that can be pointed to, despite being the step on which the outcome depended.

Where does the word videre come from?
Videre descends from an ancient root meaning both to see and to know, which also produced the Greek verb for knowing, the Sanskrit veda meaning knowledge, and the English words wit and wise.

Why did CZARD name a watch VIDI?
 VIDI represents the stage of making something that consumes the most time and receives the least recognition, the period of judgement between beginning a piece of work and completing it. It is the second chapter in a trilogy that follows the sequence of the phrase itself.

entry.title: Why CZARD Chose a Sellita Movement: The Swiss Mechanical Heart of GENEVE
entry.summary:
Discover why CZARD selected the Swiss Sellita movement for the GENÈVE collection, and how that decision reflects our philosophy of precision, reliability, and lasting mechanical craftsmanship.

More
entry.content:
The Heart You Never See

Every great watch is judged twice.

First by what the eye sees.

Then, over years of ownership, by what the eye never can.

The dial catches the light. The case reflects its surroundings. The hands move with quiet certainty. Together, they create the first impression, the visible language through which every watch introduces itself.

Yet the true measure of a watch begins elsewhere.

Hidden beneath the dial is a precisely engineered mechanism that most owners will never see. Springs, gears and carefully manufactured components work together with remarkable consistency, determining not only how a watch keeps time, but how it feels to own, how confidently it performs and how naturally it becomes part of everyday life.

That mechanism is the movement.

Collectors understand this instinctively. They admire design, but place their trust in engineering. Long after the novelty of a polished case has faded, the movement simply continues doing what it was built to do, determining whether a watch deserves to remain on the wrist for years rather than months.

For more than a century, the movement has been the clearest expression of a watchmaker's philosophy. It reveals the standards a brand refuses to compromise, the traditions it chooses to preserve and the engineering it believes will endure long after changing fashions have disappeared. These decisions rarely announce themselves. They simply become part of ownership.

That is why serious watchmaking has always begun from within.

The creation of GENEVE followed the same principle.

Before considering proportions, finishes or the character of the dial, there was a more important question.


What should power it?

The answer was never driven by novelty or marketing. It was guided by a belief that the movement should embody the same principles as the watch surrounding it: precision, dependability, enduring craftsmanship and a genuine respect for one of the world's most admired traditions of horology.

At CZARD, every collection begins with a single question: what deserves to endure? Every decision that follows exists to answer it.

That search naturally led to Switzerland.

More specifically, it led to Sellita.

Among watch enthusiasts, Sellita is a name associated with understated credibility. It rarely appears on the dial itself, yet its Swiss mechanical movements have earned the confidence of respected independent manufacturers and established Swiss maisons alike. That reputation has been built through dependable engineering, long-term serviceability and decades of consistent performance rather than publicity.

The significance of that decision extends far beyond engineering.

It reflects a philosophy in which quality is measured before it is seen, thoughtful choices matter more than visible claims and every component earns its place because it contributes to the whole.

Those principles have shaped Swiss watchmaking for generations.

They also shape the philosophy behind GENEVE.

 

 

What a Swiss Mechanical Automatic Really Is

Modern life has made precision almost invisible. Phones synchronise automatically, computers reference atomic clocks and digital devices keep exceptionally accurate time while asking almost nothing from the people who use them.

From a purely practical perspective, telling the time has never been easier.

Yet mechanical watches continue to occupy a place that technology has never replaced because they offer a fundamentally different experience.

A Swiss automatic movement is powered not by electronics or a battery, but by mechanical energy. As the watch is worn, the natural motion of the wrist turns an oscillating rotor that gradually winds the mainspring. The stored energy is then released through a carefully regulated system of gears and components, allowing the watch to measure time through mechanical precision alone.

Every passing second is the result of physical engineering rather than electronic calculation.

That changes the relationship between owner and object.

A mechanical watch becomes part of everyday life.

Over time, owners begin to appreciate qualities that rarely appear on a specification sheet: the smooth rhythm of the seconds hand, the reassuring feel of a winding crown and the confidence that hundreds of carefully engineered components continue working together beneath the dial with remarkable consistency.

These are subtle experiences that reward patience rather than instant gratification.

Swiss watchmaking has spent generations refining this philosophy. Precision has always mattered, but precision alone has never been the objective. The greater ambition has been to create Swiss mechanical movements that unite engineering, craftsmanship and long-term dependability into something capable of lasting far beyond the generation that first assembled it.

For collectors, this distinction is fundamental. Two watches may appear remarkably similar from the outside, yet their movements shape entirely different ownership experiences. They influence reliability, servicing, longevity and, perhaps most importantly, the connection that develops between owner and watch over many years.

The finest watches are admired for their appearance.

They are remembered for what powers them.

That pursuit of enduring craftsmanship naturally leads to one of Switzerland's most respected movement manufacturers.

Sellita.

The Name Behind the Movement

For many people discovering mechanical watches, the name on the dial is the first thing they notice.

Collectors often begin somewhere else.

They begin with the movement.

A dial introduces a watch, but the movement reveals the standards behind it. The company that designs and manufactures that movement becomes part of the watch's identity, even when its name remains hidden beneath the caseback.

Within Swiss watchmaking, Sellita occupies precisely that position.

It is one of Switzerland's most respected movement manufacturers, trusted by independent watchmakers and established maisons alike. Although its name rarely appears on the front of a watch, its engineering powers thousands of mechanical timepieces valued for their consistency, dependability and long-term serviceability.

Its story begins in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, one of the historic centres of Swiss watchmaking.

For generations, the city developed around a unique ecosystem of movement manufacturers, component specialists, dial makers, case manufacturers and master watchmakers. Skills were refined over decades and passed from one generation to the next, creating an environment where precision became part of the culture rather than simply a manufacturing standard.

Founded in 1950, Sellita initially specialised in assembling Swiss mechanical movements for other manufacturers. The work demanded exceptional discipline. Every component had to meet exact tolerances, every assembled movement had to perform consistently and every process reflected the standards expected of Swiss horology.

For decades, Sellita worked behind the scenes. Its name was rarely known outside the industry, yet its craftsmanship appeared inside watches carrying many different names.

There is something fitting about that.

The finest craftsmanship often remains invisible to the person who ultimately enjoys it. Sellita earned its reputation not through publicity, but through decades of dependable engineering that supported the work of respected watchmakers around the world.

One of the defining chapters in the company's history came through its long relationship with ETA, one of Switzerland's best-known movement manufacturers.

For many years, Sellita assembled ETA movements under licence, gaining deep expertise in Swiss mechanical movement production while working to exceptionally demanding standards. That experience later became the foundation for expanding its own manufacturing capabilities.

The landscape of Swiss watchmaking changed during the early twenty-first century.

As ETA gradually reduced the supply of movements to many external brands, independent watchmakers faced an important challenge. The industry needed another manufacturer capable of producing Swiss mechanical movements with the same commitment to quality, consistency and long-term reliability.

Sellita was uniquely prepared.

Decades of accumulated expertise allowed the company to expand its own production and become one of the most respected movement manufacturers serving the broader Swiss watch industry.

That transition represented more than increased production.

It represented trust.

In watchmaking, trust is earned over decades rather than claimed overnight. A movement is expected to perform not merely for months, but for years of everyday wear, regular servicing and continuous operation. Brands whose reputations have been built over generations cannot afford uncertainty beneath the dial.

That is why Sellita today powers watches from respected names across the industry.

Brands such as Oris, Sinn, TAG Heuer and IWC have all used Sellita movements within selected collections, reflecting the confidence placed in the company's engineering and manufacturing standards.

Collectors recognise the significance of that confidence. Not because a movement is fashionable, but because respected watchmakers choose it willingly. Confidence between manufacturers is rarely built on advertising. It is built on performance, consistency and the ability to deliver the same standard year after year.

That is what Sellita has achieved.

Its reputation rests not on visibility, but on decades of dependable engineering.

Those values align naturally with the philosophy behind GENEVE.

For GENEVE, that confidence begins long before the hands begin to move.

It begins with Sellita.

Why CZARD Chose Sellita

Every watch is the result of hundreds of decisions.

Some are immediately visible. The proportions of the case, the typography of the dial and the finish of the hands all contribute to its character. Others remain hidden beneath the surface, yet they shape the ownership experience far more profoundly than anything visible at first glance.

Choosing a movement is not simply selecting the mechanism that measures time.

It is deciding what principles will define the watch for years to come.

For CZARD, the creation of GENEVE began with that understanding.

Before refinement could be expressed through design, it first had to exist within the watch itself. That is why GENEVE is powered by a Swiss Sellita mechanical automatic movement.

The decision was never made because Sellita is a recognised name, nor because the words Swiss Made carry prestige on a specification sheet. It was made because the movement reflected the values CZARD wanted GENEVE to embody.

The first is craftsmanship.

Swiss mechanical watchmaking has earned its reputation not through marketing, but through generations of disciplined engineering. Every movement represents hundreds of carefully considered decisions working together with remarkable precision. The finished watch becomes the visible expression of craftsmanship that exists beneath the surface.

The second is dependability.

A mechanical watch is created with the expectation that it will remain part of its owner's life for many years. Confidence comes not from how loudly a watch announces itself, but from how consistently it performs through ordinary moments. Reliability is rarely dramatic. It simply becomes something the owner learns to trust.

The third is serviceability.

Unlike many modern products designed to be replaced, a mechanical watch is built with longevity in mind. It is expected to be maintained, cared for and appreciated over time. That tradition remains one of the defining characteristics of fine watchmaking and reflects a belief that quality should be sustained rather than consumed.

These qualities made Sellita an appropriate foundation for GENEVE. Not because it was fashionable. Not because it was expected. Rather, because it had earned the confidence of the wider Swiss watch industry through decades of consistent engineering and dependable mechanical performance.

That distinction matters because luxury has never been defined by excess.

Swiss watchmaking suggests something different. It values restraint, precision and the confidence to choose what matters while leaving everything unnecessary behind.

The same philosophy guides thoughtful design in every discipline. The finest architecture is remembered for its proportions rather than ornament. The finest tailoring is admired for its fit rather than decoration. The finest objects are appreciated because nothing exists without a reason.

That belief defines GENEVE.

Every visible detail has been considered carefully, while every hidden decision carries equal importance. The movement's purpose extends far beyond the specification sheet, forming the foundation upon which every other decision rests.

Each CZARD collection is developed according to its own character and purpose. The movement is chosen because it best serves the watch it powers, not because every watch should be built in exactly the same way.

GENEVE expresses that philosophy through its Swiss Sellita mechanical automatic movement.

Swiss watchmaking has held to the same standard for generations. Its greatest achievements have rarely been the loudest. They have simply endured the longest.

Every design ultimately begins with a simple question.

Does this decision genuinely improve the watch?

If the answer is no, it has no place.

If the answer is yes, it deserves to remain, whether immediately visible or hidden within the watch itself.

That principle explains every decision behind GENEVE.

Long after the dial has been admired.

Long after the case has gathered the marks of years.

The movement simply continues doing what it was built to do.

That is the difference between wearing a watch and owning one built to endure.

 

 

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Sellita movement?

A Sellita movement is a Swiss mechanical movement manufactured by Sellita SA in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland. Sellita movements are widely respected for their reliability, precision, and long-term serviceability, making them a trusted choice for many independent and established Swiss watch brands.

What movement does the CZARD GENEVE use?

GENEVE is powered by a Swiss Sellita mechanical automatic movement, chosen for its precision, dependability and long-term serviceability.


Do all CZARD watches use Swiss movements?

No. Each CZARD collection is developed according to its own character and purpose. GENEVE is powered by a Swiss Sellita mechanical automatic movement, while the VENI, VIDI and VICI collections use a VK64 meca-quartz movement.

Is Sellita a Swiss company?

Yes. Sellita is a Swiss movement manufacturer founded in 1950 and based in La Chaux-de-Fonds, one of the historic centres of Swiss watchmaking.

Why do collectors trust Sellita movements?

Collectors value Sellita movements because they have earned a reputation for dependable mechanical performance, consistent manufacturing quality and straightforward long-term servicing. Their widespread adoption by respected Swiss brands has further reinforced that confidence.

What is the difference between Sellita and ETA?

Sellita and ETA are both established Swiss movement manufacturers. Sellita assembled ETA movements under licence for many years before expanding its own manufacturing capabilities. Today, both companies produce respected Swiss mechanical movements used throughout the watch industry.

Why do independent watch brands choose Sellita?

Many independent brands choose Sellita because its movements combine Swiss manufacturing, proven engineering, long-term serviceability and dependable mechanical performance. These qualities allow brands to focus on creating distinctive watches while relying on a trusted mechanical foundation.

 

 

The finest watches are remembered for what they become over time, not simply for what they promise on the day they are made.

History gives a watch its context.

Craftsmanship gives it its character.

The movement gives it life.

The years give it meaning.

That is the quiet promise of every great mechanical watch.

 

 


Explore the World of CZARD

History informs every collection. Thoughtful design shapes every watch. Continue exploring the ideas behind CZARD.
